# Sarvesh Mohite's blog, full text

# My coding agent kept re-reading the internet

URL: https://blog.sarveshmohite.me/building-u2md/
Published: 2026-11-24
Tags: go, agents, crawlers

> Inside u2md: turning docs sites into local Markdown an agent can actually use, one cache shared by every repo on the machine, and the four tildes of a Python traceback that broke search.

Every time my coding agent needed a docs page, it went and fetched it. The same page, from the same site, in every repo
and every session. Then it read all ten thousand tokens of it, sidebar included, to find the one paragraph it wanted.

[u2md](https://github.com/CyberSarvesh/u2md) is what I built instead: one Go binary that turns a documentation site into
clean Markdown **once**, keeps it on your machine, and hands an agent only the part it asked for. It started this month
as a crawler and grew into something closer to a local library for docs. Almost everything worth writing about came
from pointing it at real sites and watching it be wrong.

<figure class="ux" role="img" aria-label="Terminal: u2md mirrors 30 pages of docusaurus.io, skipping 1058 pages from 12 older doc versions. Run again with a max age of one hour, all 30 pages come from the local store with no network requests.">
<style>

## The shape of it

<figure class="um" role="img" aria-label="u2md architecture. An agent asks u2md through the CLI or the MCP server. u2md first checks a shared store of raw responses kept by content hash; a fresh copy is served with no network. Only a stale copy is revalidated against the docs site, usually with a 304. Pages are converted into Markdown with an index, sections and token counts. Other repos on the same machine reuse the store with zero requests, and a pack carries docs and cache to a teammate or CI with no network.">
<style>

<div class="um-key"><span class="ok"><i></i>local, no network</span><span class="net"><i></i>network, only when stale</span><span class="pk"><i></i>sharing, no network</span></div>

One rule shapes the whole thing: **the network is the slow, unreliable part, so touch it as little as possible.** A page
is downloaded once, stored under the hash of its contents, and turned into Markdown from there. Every read after that
is local.

## Extraction is mostly deleting things

A docs page is maybe a third documentation. The rest is sidebar, navbar, version picker, cookie banner, "Edit this
page" and "Was this helpful?". u2md recognises Docusaurus, MkDocs Material, Mintlify, Sphinx and VitePress by their DOM
markers and knows what to cut from each. Anything else falls back to `main`, `article` or `[role=main]`.

Knowing what to cut was the easy half. Knowing what **not** to cut took real sites. In my first run against
docusaurus.io:

| on 30 docusaurus.io pages | first run | now |
|---|---|---|
| pages missing their title | 18 | 0 |
| pages that were old-version copies | 18 | 0 |
| callouts | a bare word: `tip` | `> **Tip**` |

The titles were a lovely bug. Docusaurus puts a page's only `<h1>` inside a `<header>`, and deleting `<header>` is the
first thing every extractor does. So the title left with the site chrome. Now the `h1` gets lifted out first, unless
the page has another one.

The versions were worse. docusaurus.io keeps a full copy of its docs for every release (`/docs/2.x/`, `/docs/3.0.1/`,
a dozen more), and those sort before the current docs. A 30-page crawl spent most of its budget on near-identical old
copies. Directories named like dotted versions, or `next`, are now skipped by default with a warning that lists them.
Bare integers like `/v1/` are left alone, because those are usually API versions rather than duplicates.

Python's docs were wrong more quietly. They use Sphinx's classic theme, which has none of the markers I'd taught it, so
every page fell back to the generic extractor. The output still looked fine, which is exactly why nobody noticed. It
knows the classic theme now.

## Links are the hard part

Converting HTML to Markdown is a library call. Making the links work afterwards is not. A page links to
`/docs/install`, which redirects to `/docs/install/`, whose canonical URL is `/docs/installation`, and all three have
to land on the same local file.

So conversion runs in two passes. The first keeps every link absolute and only collects them. When the crawl is done
and every redirect, canonical and dead link is known, the second pass rewrites links through
[goldmark](https://github.com/yuin/goldmark)'s syntax tree instead of a regex. That's the difference between rewriting
a link and "fixing" a URL that happened to appear inside a code sample.

## The same page, byte for byte

Mirror the same site twice and you get identical files. The crawl goes level by level with each level sorted, and
everything after the download comes from the cached bytes, so `--offline` rebuilds are identical too.

The sneaky enemy was the date. Every page's frontmatter records when it was fetched, and servers without `ETag` or
`Last-Modified` look new on every request. So every file changed every day, and every changelog was a list of nothing.
Now `fetched_at` means "first seen": if the body hashes the same as the cached one, the old date stays.

That sounds like pedantry until you commit docs to git. Then a diff only shows up when the docs actually changed.

## Four tildes broke my search

Search is BM25 over heading-sized chunks. I tested it on the Python tutorial with *how do I handle exceptions with
finally*, and the section that explains `finally` didn't make the top five.

It wasn't the ranking. One chunk, "8.2 Exceptions", was 18,234 characters long. It had swallowed sections 8.3 to 8.7
whole, including the one I was looking for. The culprit was in a code block a few lines down:

```text
>>> '2' + 2
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
    '2' + 2
    ~~~~^~~
TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str
```

That last caret line is Python pointing at the bad expression. Here's how my splitter decided what was code:

```go
// the old splitter, trimmed
if strings.HasPrefix(trim, "```") || strings.HasPrefix(trim, "~~~") {
	inFence = !inFence
}
```

`~~~~^~~` starts with three tildes. So the parser thought the code block ended there, treated the real closing fence as
the start of a new one, and read every heading after it as code. Five sections became one, and the answer drowned in it.

Markdown has an actual rule for this. A fence only closes on a line made of the **same** character, at least as many
of them, and nothing else:

```go
func (f fence) closes(line string) bool {
	s, ok := trimIndent(line)
	if !ok {
		return false
	}
	n := 0
	for n < len(s) && s[n] == f.char {
		n++
	}
	return n >= f.n && strings.TrimSpace(s[n:]) == ""
}
```

The fix that mattered more was structural. Headings, fences and anchors are now decided in exactly one package, which
search, filters and section reads all share. So an anchor that search returns is always one that `read_section` can
open. The `finally` section ranks first now.

While I was in there, the stemmer turned out to file *handle* and *handling* under different words. Search bugs are
like that: they never crash, they just make you a little worse at finding things.

## Download once per machine

Every repo used to keep its own cache. Now there's one store per machine (`~/.cache/u2md` on Linux), with raw
responses kept by content hash. And with a `max_age`, a recent copy is served before anything else happens:

```go
if f.opt.MaxAge > 0 {
	if r, ok := f.lookup(norm); ok && time.Since(r.CheckedAt) < f.opt.MaxAge {
		return r, nil
	}
}
```

That check runs before DNS and before `robots.txt`. The robots file needed reading-through too, including the "this
site has none" answer, or every warm run would still make one request per host. Copies older than `max_age` are
revalidated with `ETag`/`Last-Modified`, which is usually a cheap `304`. If the server is down, the agent gets the last
copy marked `cache: stale`. A refusal is never covered up that way. A 404, a robots rule or the SSRF guard saying no
stays an error, and a `robots.txt` that couldn't be *reached* is a different error from one that said no.

Sharing the store broke something, of course. Each process loaded the index, added its entries and wrote its whole
snapshot back on exit, so the last process to finish erased everyone else's work. It's the same lost update as the
[zombie worker in TaskForge](../building-taskforge/) wearing different clothes. Now a flush takes a lock file,
re-reads what's on disk and writes back only the keys it changed.

## Agents don't need the whole page

Every mirrored site starts with an `INDEX.md` listing pages with token counts, so an agent can budget before reading.
That still meant reading whole pages, so there are now three smaller ways in:

- **`read_section`** returns one section and its subsections, by `page.md#anchor`.
- **`get_context`** packs the best-matching sections into a token budget.
- **`find_examples`** returns only the code blocks, which is often all an agent wanted.

Here's the start of `get_context` with a budget of 600 tokens, on that same question:

```text
<!-- u2md context: 2 sections, ~599 of 600 tokens, 11 relevant sections did not fit -->

## 8. Errors and Exceptions > 8.7. Defining Clean-up Actions
Source: 3/tutorial/errors.md#87-defining-clean-up-actions
```

Packing goes in rank order. A section that doesn't fit is skipped, but smaller ones below it still get a chance. It
stops once matches fall under a quarter of the best score, because past that point it's filler, not context. If even
the best section is too big on its own, it's cut on a line or word boundary and marked as cut (closing any code fence
it interrupted), so the answer is never empty. And it says what it left out, so the agent knows to ask for more.

## Configure once

Flags are fine for a person and annoying for an agent, which has to remember them every call. So a `u2md.yaml` in the
repo, plus an optional global one, holds the settings:

```yaml
defaults:
  max_age: 7d
  drop_sections: ['Was this helpful?', 'Changelog*']

sites:
  - url: https://docs.stripe.com/api
    keep_sections: ['Parameters', 'Returns']
```

The CLI and the MCP server both pick it up, so the agent never passes a setting. Unknown keys are an error, because a
typo that silently does nothing is the worst kind. Pages converted with filters record a hash of the rules in their
frontmatter, so a filtered copy is never mistaken for the real thing.

## Sharing without the network

`u2md pack` bundles the Markdown together with the raw responses behind it into one file. Packing the same tree twice
gives the same bytes, so packs diff cleanly. The 17-page Python tutorial came to 265 KB.

A teammate with an empty cache can unpack it and rebuild with `--offline`, and get the original files byte for byte.
I checked. Since a pack can come from anywhere, unpacking is defensive: every body must hash to its own name, nothing
may land outside the target folder, only Markdown goes under `docs/`, and an old pack can never replace a newer local
copy.

## A crawler you can't point inward

A tool that fetches whatever URL an agent hands it is an SSRF bug waiting for a prompt. So u2md resolves a host once,
refuses it if any address is private, loopback or link-local, and then connects to the checked IP instead of the
hostname, so DNS can't answer differently the second time. Every redirect gets the same check, and proxy settings are
ignored on purpose, because a proxy would make the check meaningless.

It also has to explain itself. For a while, blocking `localtest.me` said `disallowed by robots.txt`, because fetching
`robots.txt` is what hit the guard first. Now it says:

```text
u2md: error: fetch: blocked by SSRF guard: localtest.me -> 127.0.0.1 (pass --allow-private to permit private, loopback or link-local hosts)
```

## Try it

You need Go 1.26 or newer:

```bash
go install github.com/CyberSarvesh/u2md/cmd/u2md@latest
u2md mirror https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/ -o docs --max-pages 25
u2md context docs/docs.python.org "how do I handle exceptions with finally" --budget 1500
```

To give it to Claude Code or Cursor, add it to your MCP config:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "u2md": { "command": "u2md", "args": ["mcp", "--dir", ".u2md-docs"] }
  }
}
```

Some honest limits:

- **No JavaScript.** Docs that only exist after a browser runs a script come out empty. u2md warns when a page looks
  like that, but it can't fix it.
- **Search is words, not meaning.** BM25 and a small stemmer are deterministic and fast, and they miss synonyms.
- **Token counts are estimates**, at about four characters a token.
- One known leftover: docusaurus.io's `/docs/next` landing page still gets mirrored next to the current one.

## What I'd add next

- **Section-level changelogs** for `sync`, so "the docs changed" becomes "the section on retries changed".
- **Opt-in rendering** for the JavaScript-only sites, kept out of the default path.
- **Better ranking for short, precise sections**, which still lose to long ones that mention everything.

> The network is the part you can't fix. Use it once, keep the bytes, and make everything after that local.

The code is [on GitHub](https://github.com/CyberSarvesh/u2md). If you have a docs site it mangles, that's the issue I
most want to read.

---

# My terminal has movie posters now

URL: https://blog.sarveshmohite.me/building-tuinime/
Published: 2026-11-22
Tags: rust, tui, async

> Inside TuiNime, an anime TUI in Rust: one event loop, background tasks, pictures made of text, and a release built from a git tag.

Terminals are very good at text. An anime browser is mostly pictures, search boxes and waiting for the network, which
are three things text grids are not famous for.

[TuiNime](https://github.com/CyberSarvesh/TuiNime) is my attempt at one anyway: a Rust TUI where you browse what's
trending, search as you type, pick an episode, and hand playback to [mpv](https://mpv.io). The interesting part turned
out to be **everything that has to happen without freezing the screen**.

![TuiNime browsing trending shows, searching, opening an episode list and switching themes](https://blog.sarveshmohite.me/media/tuinime/demo.gif)

## The shape of it

<figure class="tn" role="img" aria-label="TuiNime architecture. An event loop takes input, draws to the terminal through ratatui and starts mpv for playback, without waiting on the network. It spawns tokio tasks that call AniList and the providers over HTTP and send results back as BgEvent messages.">

<div class="tn-key"><span class="ok"><i></i>instant</span><span class="slow"><i></i>background work</span><span class="net"><i></i>network</span></div>

[ratatui](https://ratatui.rs) draws the interface, [tokio](https://tokio.rs) runs the slow work, and mpv does the one
job I have no business rewriting: playing video.

## Never wait in the event loop

If the loop that reads the keyboard also waits for HTTP, a slow server means a dead keyboard. So every network call
gets its own task, and the only way back is a message:

```rust
pub fn spawn_search(catalog: Catalog, tx: UnboundedSender<BgEvent>, seq: u64, query: String) {
    tokio::spawn(async move {
        let result = catalog.search(&query, 20).await.map_err(|e| format!("{e:#}"));
        let _ = tx.send(BgEvent::Search { seq, query, result });
    });
}
```

The main loop waits for whichever happens first, a result or some input:

```rust
// trimmed
let ev = tokio::select! {
    Some(bg) = app.next_background() => {
        app.on_background(bg).await;
        continue;
    }
    ev = events.next() => ev,
};
```

It's the same idea as [my API that never sends emails](../never-send-email-in-a-request/): accept the work, return
straight away, deliver the result later. The "client" is just a person holding the down arrow.

## Responses arrive in the wrong order

Live search waits for a 350 ms pause in typing before it sends anything. That cuts down on requests, but it doesn't
order them: the search for `fri` can still finish after the search for `frieren`.

So each search carries the `seq` number you saw above, and a result with an old number is dropped:

```rust
if seq != self.search.seq {
    return; // superseded by a newer search
}
```

## Pictures made of text

Some terminals can show real images, through the Kitty, Sixel or iTerm2 protocols. For the rest there is a lovely
trick: the character `▀` fills the top half of a cell. Give it a foreground and a background color and each cell
becomes two pixels.

TuiNime uses [ratatui-image](https://github.com/ratatui/ratatui-image) to ask the terminal what it supports at
startup, with half-blocks as the fallback. Two details matter around it:

- **Encoding is expensive**, so encoded posters are cached by `(url, width, height)` and not redone every frame.
- **Sixel pixels aren't cells.** ratatui erases by diffing cells, so it can't see them. The screen is cleared whenever
  the view changes, or old posters would haunt the next one.

![The details screen, with a poster drawn in half-blocks next to the synopsis and episode grid](https://blog.sarveshmohite.me/media/tuinime/details.png)

## The same show has three names

AniList knows a show by its English, romaji and native titles. A provider usually knows one of them, and its IDs mean
nothing to AniList. So TuiNime searches by each name, lowercases and strips the punctuation, and ranks what comes back:

| match | rank |
|---|---|
| exact | 3 |
| one is a prefix of the other | 2 |
| one contains the other | 1 |
| none of these | 0 |

Ties go to the closest length. It's not clever, and that is what I like about it: when it picks wrong, I can see why.

Providers also go down, so they all sit behind one trait. If the first can't produce a playable link, the next gets
the same show and episode number, and the status bar says who failed.

## Don't print. Ever.

In a TUI, stderr and the interface share a screen, so one stray warning scribbles over the layout. TuiNime logs to a
file instead, and a panic hook puts the terminal back before the error prints:

```rust
// trimmed
std::panic::set_hook(Box::new(move |info| {
    let _ = disable_raw_mode();
    let _ = execute!(std::io::stdout(), DisableMouseCapture, LeaveAlternateScreen);
    orig_hook(info);
}));
```

A crash should cost you the app, not the terminal.

## Shipping is a git tag

[dist](https://github.com/axodotdev/cargo-dist) generates the release workflow. Pushing `v0.1.0` built binaries for
Windows, Linux and macOS, published them with checksums and installers, and updated my Homebrew tap.

You need [mpv](https://mpv.io/installation/) on your `PATH`. Then, on macOS or Linux with Homebrew:

```bash
brew install CyberSarvesh/tap/tuinime
```

Or on Windows, in PowerShell:

```powershell
powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -c "irm https://github.com/CyberSarvesh/TuiNime/releases/latest/download/tuinime-installer.ps1 | iex"
```

TuiNime doesn't host any video. The providers are unofficial third-party sites that I don't control, so check what is
licensed and legal where you live, and pay for the shows you love.

## What I'd add next

- **Decode posters off the render path.** Network work is in the background, but decoding a cached image still
  happens while drawing.
- **More package managers**, so installing is one familiar command everywhere.
- **Licensed sources**, wherever one offers a way in for a client like this.

> The general rule: the loop that draws the screen should never be the one doing the waiting.

The code is [on GitHub](https://github.com/CyberSarvesh/TuiNime). Issues, and corrections to my Rust, are welcome.

---

# hello, world (from PID 1)

URL: https://blog.sarveshmohite.me/hello-world/
Published: 2026-11-14
Tags: meta

> Why this blog exists, what I plan to write about, and why it lives on its own subdomain.

Every developer blog starts with a post about starting a blog. This is that post.

## What goes here

Mostly backend things I've built, broken, or finally understood:

- **Queues and workers.** Why the slow part of a request shouldn't be in the request.
- **Databases.** Postgres, indexes, and why `SELECT *` keeps showing up in my nightmares.
- **Systems programming.** I'm learning C and Rust the slow way, and I'll write down what I learn as I go.
- **Post-mortems.** Mine, of my own projects. Friendly ones.

## Why a subdomain?

The portfolio at `sarveshmohite.me` is the brochure. `blog.sarveshmohite.me` is the notebook. Both are built from
one Astro codebase, so the notebook gets the same theme and command palette (press <kbd>Ctrl</kbd> + <kbd>K</kbd>).

## How to reach me

If something here is wrong, and some of it will be, tell me. The email is at the bottom of every post.

```bash
$ whoami
sarvesh
$ echo "first post" >> /var/log/sarvesh.log
```

# My API never sends emails (and yours shouldn’t either)

URL: https://blog.sarveshmohite.me/never-send-email-in-a-request/
Published: 2026-11-10
Tags: backend, queues, redis, postgres

> What I learned building TaskForge: move slow work out of the request path with Postgres, Redis and a pool of workers.

Some endpoints do a lot of work: send an email, build a PDF, resize an image, call a slow third-party API. If you do
that work **inside** the request, the client waits for all of it, and your server holds a connection open the whole
time. Ten slow requests at once and everything else queues up behind them.

[TaskForge](https://github.com/CyberSarvesh/TaskForge) is my small demo of the fix: **accept the job, store it, return
straight away, and let workers do the work.**

## The shape of it

```text
client --POST /jobs--> api --INSERT--------> postgres  (source of truth)
                        |
                        +--LPUSH id--> redis            (just the queue)
                                         |
                                         | BRPOP
                                         v
                                      workers --UPDATE status--> postgres
```

The API does two cheap things and replies `202 Accepted`:

1. Writes the job (type, payload, `status = 'queued'`) to PostgreSQL.
2. Pushes the job's **ID**, not its payload, onto a Redis list.

## The API side

```ts
app.post('/jobs', async (req, res) => {
  const { type, payload } = req.body;

  const { rows } = await db.query(
    `INSERT INTO jobs (type, payload, status) VALUES ($1, $2, 'queued') RETURNING id`,
    [type, payload],
  );

  await redis.lPush('jobs', rows[0].id);
  res.status(202).json({ id: rows[0].id, status: 'queued' });
});
```

The handler finishes in a few milliseconds however slow the job is.

## The worker side

```ts
while (true) {
  const item = await redis.brPop('jobs', 0); // blocks until something arrives
  const job = await getJob(item.element);

  await setStatus(job.id, 'running');
  try {
    await handlers[job.type](job.payload);
    await setStatus(job.id, 'done');
  } catch (err) {
    await setStatus(job.id, 'failed', String(err));
  }
}
```

`BRPOP` blocks, so idle workers cost almost nothing. Need more throughput? Start more worker processes. They all pull
from the same list and Redis gives each job to exactly one of them.

## Why Postgres *and* Redis?

Redis is a great queue, but I don't want it to be the only record that a job exists. Postgres holds the durable state
(what was asked for, when, and what happened), so a `GET /jobs/:id` endpoint can report status even after Redis has
forgotten the ID.

## What I'd add next

- **Retries with backoff**, using an `attempts` column and a delayed re-queue.
- **A reaper** for jobs stuck in `running` after a worker crash.
- **Idempotency keys**, so a client retrying `POST /jobs` doesn't enqueue the same email twice.

> The general rule: if the user doesn't need the result to read the response, it doesn't belong in the request.

The hero animation on my [homepage](https://sarveshmohite.me) is this exact flow. Click **POST /jobs** a few times and
watch the queue fill up.

---

# My job queue said completed. It was lying.

URL: https://blog.sarveshmohite.me/building-taskforge/
Published: 2026-05-22 · Updated: 2026-11-22
Tags: backend, queues, postgres, redis

> Inside TaskForge: the small queue I built in March, the ways it lost work, and the November rebuild with leases, fencing tokens and a factory floor you can break.

A job queue has one promise to keep: if it says it has your job, your job happens. It's a very easy promise to make in
sixty lines of TypeScript, and a surprisingly easy one to break in the same sixty.

[TaskForge](https://github.com/CyberSarvesh/TaskForge) started that small in March 2026, as an API, a Redis list and
one worker. **The frontend is recent.** It was built in November 2026, along with the rewrite that made the backend
survive crashes, and this post was updated to cover both. So it's a story in two halves: the queue as it was, and what
it took to make it honest.

![Jobs flowing across the TaskForge factory floor, a worker being killed, and the other workers finishing its jobs](https://blog.sarveshmohite.me/media/taskforge/demo.gif)

## March: sixty lines of optimism

The first worker took an ID from Redis, loaded the row from Postgres and did this:

```ts
// March 2026, trimmed
await query("UPDATE jobs SET status = $1 WHERE id = $2", ["processing", jobId]);

if (job.type === "email") {
  await emailJob(job.payload);
}

if (job.type === "report") {
  await reportJob(job.payload);
}

await query(
  "UPDATE jobs SET status = $1, completed_at = NOW() WHERE id = $2",
  ["completed", jobId]
);
```

Read it again with a job of type `nonsense`. Neither `if` matches, nothing runs, and the job is marked **completed**.

That was the funny bug. These are the others that turned up when that version was finally poked properly:

| what happened | what March did | what it does now |
|---|---|---|
| unknown job type | marked it completed | rejects it |
| worker killed mid-job | processing, forever | another worker finishes it |
| Redis down | request hung, job orphaned | accepts it, runs it later |
| Postgres restarted | API crashed | reconnects |
| empty database | every request failed | migrates itself |

None of these show up on the happy path, which is the only path a demo ever takes.

## The shape of it now

<figure class="tf" role="img" aria-label="TaskForge architecture. The API commits each job to Postgres, then adds its id to Redis, and streams changes to the factory floor. Workers take ids from Redis and renew leases in Postgres. When a killed worker falls silent its lease expires and another worker takes over the job.">

The important change is who gets to be right. **Postgres holds the truth. Redis is only an index.** You can delete the
whole Redis key and lose nothing, because every worker also runs a small sweeper that puts due jobs back:

```ts
await redis.zadd(QUEUE_KEY, "NX", ...members);
```

It's a sorted set and not a list, so adding the same ID twice does nothing. That makes "not sure it's in there? add it
again" a safe repair strategy.

## A job is borrowed, never owned

A worker that dies can't tell you it died. So claiming a job only lends it out: the worker gets a lease, and renews it
with a heartbeat for as long as the job runs. A killed process stops renewing, and that silence is the signal.

```sql
SELECT id FROM jobs
WHERE status = 'processing' AND (lease_until IS NULL OR lease_until < now())
LIMIT 500 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
```

`SKIP LOCKED` is doing quiet, lovely work there. Every worker can run that sweep at the same moment and each gets
different rows, so there is no leader to elect and no leader to lose.

## The dead sometimes come back

Leases create a nastier problem. A worker frozen for fifteen seconds looks exactly like a dead one. Its job gets handed
to somebody else, and then it wakes up, finishes, and proudly writes a result over the new owner's.

So every claim comes with a random token, and every write has to show it:

```sql
-- trimmed
UPDATE jobs SET status = 'completed', result = $3::jsonb, lease_token = NULL
WHERE id = $1 AND lease_token = $2 AND status = 'processing'
```

The old token matches zero rows. The zombie can be as confident as it likes. It's the same trick as the `seq` number
that [throws away stale searches in TuiNime](../building-tuinime/), with higher stakes.

## Urgent shouldn't mean forever

Three queues for high, normal and low is the obvious design, and it starves low the day high never empties. TaskForge
has one queue, where priority is a head start measured in time:

```ts
// trimmed
const PRIORITY_OFFSET_MS = { high: -60_000, normal: 0, low: 60_000 };

export const queueScore = (priority: Priority, runAt: Date) =>
  runAt.getTime() + PRIORITY_OFFSET_MS[priority];
```

The lowest score runs first. A low job that has waited more than two minutes beats a high job that arrived just now.
That's the whole anti-starvation system: one addition.

## November: giving it a face

A backend that recovers from crashes looks exactly like a backend that never crashed, which makes it a terrible demo.
So the new frontend is a foundry. Each ingot is a real job, each hammer is a real process, and each worker has a
**Kill** button that really kills it.

![The night shift: the floor in dark mode, with a full queue and three workers hammering](https://blog.sarveshmohite.me/media/taskforge/night-shift.jpg)

There's no 3D library under it. Isometric projection is two lines of math on a canvas:

```ts
export const project = (camera: Camera, x: number, y: number, z = 0) => ({
  x: camera.originX + (x - y) * COS * camera.scale,
  y: camera.originY + ((x + y) * 0.5 - z) * camera.scale,
});
```

The tricky part was time. A Postgres trigger sends `NOTIFY` on commit and the API relays it over Server-Sent Events, so
ingots move immediately. Snapshots arrive every couple of seconds to correct anything missed. But a snapshot can be
*older* than the event you just animated, and then ingots jump backwards. So each one remembers when it last moved:

```ts
if (existing && existing.touched > asked) continue;
```

Events make it fast. Snapshots make it true.

## Testing by breaking it

Mocks would have agreed with every bug in that table, so the integration tests start a real API and real workers
against real databases, and then get mean. They kill processes, cut the connection to Redis, drop every Postgres
connection and push 500 jobs through four workers to check that each ran exactly once.

The tests got tested too: nine guarantees were broken on purpose, and the suite caught all nine.

Squeezing the whole system into one container with a tenth of a CPU, for a free demo, found one more. A burst of reads
from a single visitor could use up the connection pool and break the live view for everyone. Rate limits don't stop
that, because a burst is allowed by definition. A cap on how many lookups run at once does.

## Try to lose a job

With Docker installed:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/CyberSarvesh/TaskForge.git
cd TaskForge
docker compose up --build
```

Open `localhost:4000`, press **Rush order**, and kill a worker while it's busy.

One honest limit: this is at-least-once delivery. A worker can send an email and die before writing down that it did,
and then that email goes out twice. The real fix belongs in the handler, as an idempotency key. The email job here only
pretends to send, so your inbox is safe.

## What I'd add next

- **Batched claims**, because writing to Postgres on every transition is the first ceiling it will hit.
- **Partitioned events**, since outside the public demo the history is kept forever.
- **Something other than `NOTIFY`** at higher volume, as it serializes the commits that use it.

> The general rule: never trust a worker to tell you that it failed. Make it keep proving that it hasn't.

The code is [on GitHub](https://github.com/CyberSarvesh/TaskForge). If you find a way to lose a job, I very much want
that issue.
